faqs.q: How do I know if the droppings in my Hackensack basement are from rats?
faqs.a: Rat droppings are capsule-shaped and about half an inch long — much larger than mouse droppings — and they concentrate along walls, near food storage, and beside the grease-dark rub marks rats leave on the routes they run nightly. In Hackensack the basement evidence usually shows up first in the older apartment stock, where pipe chases connect unit to unit and a run in one basement can mean a run in several. A rat job here is three parts: trapping out the animals present, sealing the entries (a rat needs only a half-inch gap), and cutting the food and harborage that drew them. Any baiting, where it is used at all, follows New Jersey's pesticide rules.

faqs.q: I hear scratching in my Hackensack attic at night — what could it be?
faqs.a: Night scratching narrows the list: bats at dusk, flying squirrels gliding in after dark, raccoons moving heavily, or rats running a wall route. Daytime noise would point to gray squirrels instead. Fairmount's older attics produce most of Hackensack's night-noise calls, and the droppings usually settle the squirrel-versus-raccoon question in one look. Guessing wrong wastes money — the exits, timing, and sealing differ for each — so the inspection identifies the animal from droppings, entry size, and rub marks before any equipment is set.

Hackensack.wildlife_intro:
Hackensack packs several housing eras into a small footprint: pre-war colonials and twins on the side streets, brick apartment houses near Main Street, and garden-apartment complexes toward the Hackensack River meadows. The river, Borg's Woods, and the mature street canopy keep wildlife in close contact with all of it. Rats work the commercial blocks and the alleys behind them, raccoons move between Borg's Woods and nearby chimneys, and gray squirrels treat the older soffits along Prospect Avenue and the Fairmount streets as a standing invitation every fall.

Attached housing changes the math. In a rowhouse or twin, one animal in a shared attic or party-wall void is every neighbor's problem, and sealing a single unit while the adjoining roofline stays open just moves the tenant sideways. We inspect the whole run of connected rooflines where access allows, coordinate timing with neighbors when entries cross property lines, and seal the full set of openings under one plan. Older masonry party walls hide voids that let squirrels travel between houses unseen — finding those routes is most of the job in attached stock. In Hackensack, where so much housing is attached or stacked, the inspection checks the neighboring rooflines as well, because an open entry two doors down is tomorrow's entry here.

faqs.q: Why do animals keep getting into homes in Teaneck?

faqs.q: Why do I hear running in my Ridgewood ceiling every morning?
faqs.a: Daytime running, especially at dawn and mid-afternoon, points to gray squirrels — they commute. In Ridgewood the morning running usually traces to a dormer or gable on the shaded side of the house, where the oaks give squirrels a runway straight to the entry. A squirrel entry is usually a gnawed widening at a gable vent, dormer cheek, or eave return, and the repair has to replace the chewed wood and back it with metal, or the next squirrel reopens it in days. One-way doors let the animals leave on their own schedule; then the opening is closed for good.

faqs.q: I found bat droppings in my Ridgewood attic — what happens next?
faqs.a: First we confirm the colony's size and find every entry, which is usually a cluster of small gaps at the ridge, a gable vent, or lifted flashing rather than one obvious hole. The big Ridgewood attics run hot in July, which is precisely why little brown and big brown bats pick them, and why droppings often appear in the same corner season after season. Exclusion happens inside the NJ Fish & Wildlife guideline windows — April 1 to May 14 or August 1 to October 15 — using one-way exits, and the guano cleanup afterward is handled as a health material, bagged out rather than swept into the air.

Ridgewood.wildlife_intro:
Ridgewood's housing is the big, old, tree-covered kind: Dutch colonials, Tudors, and Victorians on deep lots in the Heights and around the Old Country Club section, with the Ho-Ho-Kus Brook and the Saddle River greenway threading the east side. Big attics, complex rooflines, and forty-foot oaks leaning over them make this prime squirrel and raccoon country. Gray squirrels gnaw in at dormer cheeks and gable vents, raccoons take the larger chimneys, and summer bat colonies settle into the quiet, hot attics of the older homes near the brook.

Look at the trees before blaming the roof. A limb within jumping distance is a bridge, and squirrels treat overhanging branches the way people treat a front walk. Part of lasting proofing is arbor advice: limbs cut back several feet from the roofline, ivy stripped off walls where it gives climbers a ladder, and dense shrubs against the foundation thinned so animals lose their covered approach. Chimney and vent covers handle the rest. Houses under heavy canopy are never one-visit houses — the pressure is constant, so the sealing has to be thorough rather than quick. Ridgewood sealing plans are drawn around the canopy: where limbs bridge to a roof, proofing the house without trimming the bridge is only half a job.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Englewood porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside after dusk and do not block the opening yourself — a skunk sealed in will spray, dig, or die under the porch, and all three are worse than the skunk. East Hill porches sit over exactly the dry, sheltered crawl voids skunks prefer, and February mating season is when Englewood homeowners meet them, usually through the dog. We take skunks out with covered, low-stress handling, then trench and screen the porch perimeter with buried hardware cloth so the next one cannot move in. Skunks are a New Jersey rabies-vector species, so distance and calm are the whole technique.

faqs.q: Are squirrels in a Englewood attic actually a fire risk?
faqs.a: They can be. Squirrels gnaw constantly to wear their teeth, and wiring, PVC, and stored paper are all fair game; chewed conductors in a hot attic are a genuine hazard, not a sales line. The older East Hill and west-side homes still have plenty of knob-and-tube-era attic runs in places, which is one more reason chewed wiring here gets flagged rather than shrugged off. Once the squirrels are out and the entries are meshed, we flag any chewed wiring we saw so an electrician can judge it — that check is part of why a squirrel job should never end at just closing the hole.

Englewood.wildlife_intro:
Englewood climbs from the flat streets near Overpeck Creek up the wooded slope of the Palisades, and the wildlife follows the slope. On the East Hill, large older homes sit in heavy woods where raccoons, skunks, and groundhogs are yard regulars; down on Grand Avenue and the west-side streets, denser older housing adds squirrels in attics and rats around the commercial edges. Flat Rock Brook cuts a green corridor through the middle of the city, and the homes backing onto it get the full rotation: porch skunks in February, chimney raccoons in April, attic squirrels by October.

Yard damage tells its own story. Groundhog burrows throw fans of excavated soil against foundations, skunks leave neat cone-shaped holes hunting grubs, and moles push ridges and mounds across lawns that were level in April. Treating the yard means reading which animal made which sign — the remedies differ completely — and fixing the conditions underneath: grub-heavy turf, brush piles, and woodpiles stacked against the house. Burrows at foundations get backfilled and screened once the animals are out; a hole simply filled with dirt is a hole an animal reopens in a night. Englewood's slope lots hide burrows in retaining walls and terraced gardens, so the yard gets the same careful circuit as the roofline here.

faqs.q: A groundhog is burrowing under my Fair Lawn foundation — how bad is that?
faqs.a: Worse than it looks. A groundhog burrow system runs many feet with several chambers, and soil removed from under a slab or footing leaves voids that crack concrete and channel water against the foundation. Along Fair Lawn's river streets the burrow is often in the bank itself with a back door into the yard, so both openings get treated, not just the one at the foundation. We trap at the active entrances, then backfill and screen the site so the next groundhog inherits a closed burrow. Groundhogs are on New Jersey's rabies-vector list — one more reason not to corner one yourself.

faqs.q: An opossum is living under my Fair Lawn deck — should I be worried?
faqs.a: Mostly about the mess, not disease: opossums are not on New Jersey's high-risk rabies list, and they are placid, slow animals that would rather play dead than fight. Radburn's quiet, planted interior blocks produce many of Fair Lawn's opossum calls; the animal is almost always commuting between a deck den and a neighbor's garden, not living in the house itself. They do shred insulation and vent ducts when they den in a crawlspace, so we take them out, clean up what they left, and screen the deck or crawlspace opening with buried hardware cloth. Check for young in the pouch season before assuming it is a solo tenant.

Fair Lawn.wildlife_intro:
Fair Lawn is a postwar borough of capes, ranches, and split-levels, with the Radburn planned community at its heart and the Saddle River running its eastern edge. The river corridor is the wildlife highway: groundhogs burrow in the banks and the yards that back onto them, raccoons commute up from the water to chimneys and trash cans, and skunks work the lawns on the quiet streets around Memorial Pool. Radburn's park-like interior paths and mature plantings give squirrels and opossums cover deep inside the borough, far from the river.

Decks and porches fail at ground level. The gap beneath a low deck is dark, dry, and sheltered enough for skunks, opossums, and groundhogs to den in, and lattice alone stops none of them. Lasting work means trenching around the structure and burying galvanized hardware cloth in an L-shape, so an animal digging at the edge meets mesh angled outward underground. Lattice or skirting goes back over the top for looks. It is unglamorous digging, and it is the difference between a den that stays empty and one that fills again every spring. Fair Lawn's low ranch and cape decks are the recurring den sites here, so porch and deck screening is part of most quotes rather than an add-on.
